The `project_id`-based relink sounds like the right primitive. I would add two guardrails so it stays safe:

- make relink a recorded alias/migration event, not only an in-place `session.directory` rewrite
- require a dry-run/count path before applying: stale session count, old directory, current worktree, project id, and conflict count

Two edge cases matter:

- one old path maps to one current worktree: safe to auto-relink
- multiple current worktrees share a plausible project id/history: require user choice

Keeping the old directory as provenance also helps later diagnostics. A session can be visible under the new project while still explaining where it was originally created.

The session viewer should probably never run an unbounded diff algorithm on open.

I would split this into two layers:

- session list / open path reads only metadata plus a bounded diff summary
- full diff rendering is lazy, size-capped, and cancellable

For the specific regression, useful tests would cover:

- a large patch that exceeds the cap
- invalid or garbled encoding
- a session with many small diffs vs one pathological diff
- renderer stays responsive and shows "diff too large to render inline"

The important behavior is row-level degradation. One bad tool result or diff should not make the whole session unrecoverable.

A display symbol alone will probably be too weak for cost reporting.

I would store currency as structured pricing metadata:

- ISO currency code, e.g. `USD`, `EUR`, `JPY`
- display symbol, optional
- pricing source: provider-reported, configured, estimated, or unknown
- timestamp/version for the price table

Then the UI can render `€` while exports and totals still know what the number means. It also prevents the more dangerous failure mode: a custom provider cost shown with a familiar symbol even though the value came from a different currency or an estimate.

I would make this a copy-target choice with a visible receipt before the clipboard write.

Useful options:

- last assistant message
- selected message
- full transcript
- full transcript with tool output omitted

For full transcript, show size and token/character count before copying, with a warning above a threshold. That prevents the "paste huge transcript into GitHub" failure without changing the default for users who rely on full-session export.

It also helps privacy: the user should know whether tool output, file paths, and prior prompts are going onto the clipboard.

Since the stable SQLite-backed session id is confirmed, I would make the per-call metadata carry the rest of the provenance too.

Something like:

```json
{
  "session_id": "...",
  "session_run_id": "...",
  "turn_id": "...",
  "tool_call_id": "...",
  "project_id": "...",
  "parent_agent_id": null
```

`session_run_id` could also be a resume epoch if that is the local concept. The important part is that memory/stateful MCP servers can distinguish "same saved conversation after resume" from "same session id, different tool call." Keep this in MCP `_meta`, not model-visible tool args, and cover both stdio and HTTP transports in regression tests.

Good point — I think the confusion is that this bug is specific to the **desktop/GUI version** (Electron), not the terminal TUI version. We tested the TUI and confirmed it doesn't freeze, so your understanding is correct for that target.

The issue is in the desktop app's `TimelineDiffView` (`packages/app/src/pages/session/timeline/message-timeline.tsx`), which directly calls the O(n²) diff algorithm without any size guard — whereas the TUI apparently handles this differently. We tested with ~10k-line diffs on the latest desktop version and the renderer freezes (we have crash dumps with the stack in `execEditLength` → `diffLines` from a 33MB minidump to back this up).

PR #33198 adds a 500-line cap with "Render Anyway" fallback, which matches the existing pattern in `SessionReview`. Longer term, the lazy/cancellable architecture you suggested would be the right direction.

Also, sorry — I should have made this clearer from the start: this bug is specific to the desktop/GUI (Electron) version. The TUI version does not have this unbounded diff issue. I've updated the issue description to reflect that.

I encountered a similar problem and dug into the source code with manual validation. I wish more info like below could be added to the official documentation to explain. I hope this helps. **The model reasoning effort has two settings in two locations: `opencode.json` and `TUI -> switch model variant`. TUI variant, if selected, will overwrite the custom agent configuration in `opencode.json`. If the TUI variant is selected as `Default`, it will use what is configured in the custom agent.** Besides, `~/.local/state/opencode/model.json` caches the TUI selection, which results in the issue mentioned above. Basically, if the user changes the TUI variant setting, such a change will be cached and reused. This results in the overwrite behaviour (TUI overwrite opencode.json for custom agent). --- I tried to validate it by running a local server to receive the opencode request sent out. I also modified the project local `opencode.json` to direct model requests to that local server. This way, I can capture the actual reasoning effort in the request sent out. Others can use a similar idea for validation.

This issue is indeed likely to be a duplicate of [#9003](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues/9003) ; however, as  #9003 appears to be closed, but not resolved -- it makes sense to to reopen it as it still seems to emerge occasionally.

## Critical Issue: System Prompt Changes Break Entire Session Cache

This is a **serious performance and cost problem** that goes beyond just AGENTS.md updates. When ANY system prompt component changes during an active session, it causes a **complete cache miss** and forces the entire session context to be re-sent to the API.

### The Problem

When system prompt is modified (whether due to AGENTS.md changes, env variable changes like workspace root or git status, or date changes at midnight), the architecture forces a re-transmission of all previously cached context:

```
[System Prompt - ORIGINAL - 200K tokens cached]
[User Message 1 - cached]
[Assistant Response 1 - cached]
[User Message 2 - cached]
[Assistant Response 2 - cached]
... (many more turns)

[System Prompt CHANGES] ❌ ENTIRE CACHE INVALIDATED
[System Prompt - MODIFIED]
[User Message 1 - RE-SENT, no cache]
[Assistant Response 1 - RE-SENT, no cache]
[User Message 2 - RE-SENT, no cache]
[Assistant Response 2 - RE-SENT, no cache]
... (entire session re-sent)
```

This is not feasible for long-running sessions with 200K+ tokens of context.

### Solution

**Don't Update System Prompt for Existing Sessions**

When rules/AGENTS.md change during an active session, the AI agent **already knows what changed because it made the change itself** (or saw it in the context). There's no need to update the system prompt:

- If the agent modifies a rule via `edit` command → it knows the change
- If the user modifies AGENTS.md → communicate via `<system-reminder>` (like Claude Code does)
- The system prompt should only reflect the original session state; rule changes are part of the conversation history

The fix likely needs two counters, not one corrected sum. Keep cumulative billing/usage counters separate from the active context-window counters used for eligibility and compaction decisions.

`cache.read` can be meaningful for cost and provider accounting, but it should not make the next prompt look like it contains 41M active tokens. A good regression would assert that repeated cached turns increase billed/cache usage while active context stays bounded by retained messages plus current tool/schema overhead.

I would make `Step.Ended.cost` carry provenance instead of treating zero as a value. Suggested shape: `cost.amount`, `cost.currency`, and `cost_source=provider_reported|price_table_estimated|unavailable|not_applicable`.

That lets v2 publish a step before pricing is implemented without telling dashboards the step was free. For Copilot, provider-reported billing should win when present; token fallback should be clearly marked estimated and include missing cache-write/cache-read bucket diagnostics.

Compaction awareness should include the range and recovery contract, not only a notification. Emit `compaction.before` with candidate message range, token budget, preserve-section hints, and full-session checkpoint id; emit `compaction.after` with summary id/hash, dropped/retained range refs, and new active-context token count.

Then agents can re-anchor from durable refs instead of trusting only the lossy summary. It also gives tools a way to audit whether compaction changed task-critical state.

A compatibility test matrix would keep this from becoming best-effort glue. For `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, and `Stop`, pin payload shape, stdin encoding, exit-code semantics, stdout/stderr handling, timeout behavior, and whether verdicts block, warn, or mutate input/output.

Also include subagent/tool-nesting cases and MCP tools, since Claude hooks often guard by tool name plus transcript path. The migration story is only credible if a hook author can predict each event boundary.

A regression can seed root session, compaction child, and restored archived session rows, then assert the sidebar list remains stable across project switches and new-session creation. Missing rows should be a visible filter/state bug, not apparent data loss.

The config loader should produce partial config plus structured warnings. Unknown root keys can emit `config.warning` with JSON path, schema version, and ignored value type; invalid known sections can fall back to defaults for that section.

Session loading should only fail for errors that make runtime unsafe, such as malformed JSON or invalid required provider credentials. A regression should prove one stray root key does not block session list, resume, or new-session creation.

ACP needs a bounded retry contract around provider failures. For `session/prompt`, emit an error event with provider, model, status/error type, attempt count, retryability, and next retry deadline; after the cap, return a JSON-RPC error and mark the session idle/error.

That keeps rate limits and invalid keys from becoming infinite CPU loops. It also gives parent clients a deterministic terminal state instead of waiting forever for a prompt response that will never arrive.

Subagent spawn should record the model resolution chain before creating the child session: requested agent type, explicit override, parent model, agent config default, global default, final provider/model, and resolution source.

If the chain resolves to undefined, fail before child creation with an actionable config error. Regression cases should cover built-in subagents inheriting the parent model, explicit per-agent overrides, missing provider config, and resume/continuation of a spawned child.

Model capabilities should be resolved per request after a model switch, not cached from the session's first model. Keep capability state keyed by provider id, model id, and provider metadata revision, then invalidate attachment validators when the active model changes.

A regression can start with a text-only model, reject image input, switch to a vision model, and assert the next image request uses the new model's capability set. Also test the reverse switch blocks images again.

Project identity should be resolved at session creation, then kept as durable metadata. Store cwd, git root or workspace root, project id source, and fallback reason when the session lands in `global`.

`/sessions` from a project directory can default to that project while offering an explicit all-projects view. For existing rows, a migration can backfill likely project ids from the recorded directory, with collision/unknown cases labeled instead of hidden.

Model provenance needs to be per turn. Separate `user_selected`, `default_resolved`, `retry_fallback`, and `synthetic_internal` model sources, and only user/default sources should update the durable session model.

If a provider stream finishes with no content, write a terminal retry/error state rather than a synthetic continuation row that looks like user intent. Regression: failed retry on fallback model, then normal user follow-up, must continue with the previous real selected model.

ACP `session/list` should preserve the distinction between "known sessions" and "sessions for this cwd." Empty params should return the first page of known sessions with project/cwd metadata; `cwd` should be an optional filter.

If the existing HTTP endpoint is project-scoped, the ACP adapter likely needs a separate unscoped query path. Tests should cover empty params, explicit cwd filter, registry-launched process cwd, pagination, and sessions with missing/unknown project ids.

Pre-flight safety should be a verdict-producing layer, not only plugin callbacks. A built-in guard can evaluate normalized tool intents and return `allow|warn|block` with rule id, reason, affected paths/commands, and whether the user can override.

Start with narrow invariants: empty Write over existing file, destructive Bash patterns, write without prior read for governed files, and workspace escape. Persist the verdict receipt so later audits can tell whether a dangerous action was blocked, warned, or never inspected.

Split remote MCP state into auth token state and transport session state. A valid OAuth token should not be treated as a valid live MCP session, and a broken session should not poison the server forever.

On tool-call failure, run a lightweight health check/reinitialize path, update status as `auth_ok_transport_dead`, `reinitializing`, or `auth_failed`, and retry with a bounded policy. Tool errors should report the exact layer that failed instead of returning a misleading permission error.

Abort needs to be a terminal session state with cancellation propagated into the loop. When Feishu marks `orphan=true`, also cancel pending tasks, clear queued prompt work, and write `session.aborted` with source, channel id, final step, and cleanup result.

The loop should check that terminal flag before re-entering step 0. Parent process death and WebSocket reconnect should not revive an aborted session unless a new user action explicitly resumes it. Add a max-loop guard as a final failsafe.

When `opencode mcp list` says connected but the agent cannot see tools, diagnostics should show the missing stage, tool count, registration namespace, agent/session id, and any filtering reason. Quota windows need explicit precedence rules. Store provider, model, weekly window state, active 5-hour window state, reset times, and block reason separately; then the UI can show whether the provider blocked on weekly exhausted, active window exhausted, or local policy.

If OpenCode intentionally lets an active window finish after weekly reaches 100%, that policy should be represented as `grace_window_active`. If Z.ai blocks immediately, expose `provider_policy_weekly_hard_stop` so users do not assume a local bug.

The sidebar can use one tool-inventory model for MCP and AXI while preserving source semantics. Each row should carry `source=mcp_server|axi_cli`, name, command/path, capability summary, last scan timestamp, availability, and whether it is invocable by the agent or display-only.

That prevents users from reading AXI tools as long-running MCP processes with toggles. It also gives future telemetry a clean join point: tool inventory changed, tool became visible, tool was invoked, or tool was merely installed.

Title generation should be modeled as an optional side effect, not part of the critical first response path. A per-model `skip-title` works, but it should also record `title_source=provided|generated|skipped_by_config|skipped_local_model`.

For local providers, defaulting to skip or defer is reasonable because the extra call can dominate latency. The session can start immediately with a fallback title, then backfill a generated title only when the provider is cheap/fast enough or the user opts in.

This needs a latency breakdown per session start. Split timings for config load, external skill scan, first model call, title generation, and final response. Then local-model users can see whether the 20s delay came from title generation, skill inventory, or provider latency.

The observed `--title test` speedup is strong evidence title generation belongs behind a skip/defer policy. A regression can assert local llama.cpp with explicit title avoids the title agent path entirely.

Read-before-write works best as a receipt, not only a boolean. Track file read receipts by resolved path, inode/mtime or content hash, read offset/range, session id, and turn id; invalidate the receipt when the file changes externally.

Then a write guard can say "blocked: no current read receipt for this file" or "warning: read is stale." That avoids a model satisfying the rule with an old grep summary or a read from a different path alias.

An enforceable AGENTS layer needs a tiny machine-readable rule schema and receipts. Parse rules into ids, scope, event, matcher, condition, verdict, and message; then emit `rule_checked` records before/after tool execution.

Keep natural-language AGENTS.md separate from enforceable blocks so normal guidance does not accidentally become policy. Regression cases should cover matching by path/tool, postcondition failure, malformed rule ignored with warning, and user override when allowed by rule.

Empty writes should be treated as destructive when the target exists. Before Write commits, compare target existence, previous size/hash, new byte length, and whether the model explicitly intended truncation.

If content is empty or whitespace-only and the old file was non-empty, require an explicit truncate flag or user confirmation. The tool result should include previous size/hash and new size, so accidental zero-byte overwrites are detectable and recoverable from editor/VCS history when available.

_Generated with [ax](https://github.com/Necmttn/ax)._

Bash needs command-risk classification before permission reuse. Normalize commands into actions like `git_reset_hard`, `git_clean`, `recursive_delete`, `force_push`, and `disk_format`; then require a stronger confirmation than generic Bash approval for irreversible classes.

The receipt should record raw command, normalized action, affected cwd/path/ref when detectable, risk level, and user verdict. That lets "always approve bash" still mean ordinary commands, not silent permission to destroy uncommitted work.

_Generated with [ax](https://github.com/Necmttn/ax)._

Windows process cleanup needs job-object or process-tree ownership, not only best-effort `taskkill /T` after timeout. Create the shell and descendants under an owned job when possible, track spawned child pids, and close/kill the job on timeout, abort, or session exit.

At minimum, write a process cleanup receipt with root pid, known descendants, missed/escaped pids, timeout reason, and final kill result. That makes orphan leaks visible instead of leaving users to hunt high-CPU ping/cmd processes manually.

Glob/Grep should share the same location-boundary check as Read. Resolve the requested path, canonicalize symlinks where possible, and reject any search root outside the active Location unless the user grants an explicit broader scope.

The tool result should distinguish "no matches" from "search root rejected." Regression cases: `..` traversal, symlink escape, absolute path outside workspace, allowed subdirectory, and Windows drive-letter/case variants. Search tools are read tools, but they still expose filesystem contents.

_Generated with [ax](https://github.com/Necmttn/ax)._

Read/Edit should have one text-decoding policy. For invalid UTF-8, choose one behavior and surface it explicitly: reject as binary/invalid text with byte offset, or decode lossily with a flag and forbid Edit on lossy content.

Silent replacement in Edit is dangerous because oldString matching can fail against a different byte sequence than the file actually contains. Tests should cover invalid byte in first chunk, later chunk, truncated multibyte sequence, and binary detection false negatives.

I would separate this into capability metadata instead of hard-coding provider transforms. Each custom model could declare request fields for reasoning/thinking, allowed values, disabled form, token-budget field, and response usage buckets. Then OpenCode can validate config before the first call and normalize telemetry as reasoning/thinking output without assuming OpenAI or Anthropic field names.

This needs two independent guards: preflight on tool inventory and bounded retry. Before sending, compute tool_count, tool_schema_bytes, provider/tool limit if known, and request body size, then fail with the top contributors when over limit. After a 5xx with unchanged request hash, retry should cap quickly and mark terminal_failure instead of replaying the same oversized payload for hours.

Import should detect encoding before schema parsing and return a decode error, not file-not-found. A small import report would help: source runtime/version if present, detected encoding/BOM, normalized encoding, schema version, preserved session id, imported messages/tools, and skipped rows. That keeps UTF-16 exports from the older TypeScript runtime compatible without hiding real schema migration failures.

Broad copy tasks need a destination-aware secret guard. Before moving files into a served or world-readable path, classify obvious secret-bearing names and contents, then return a per-file plan: copy, skip, or ask. The receipt should include source path, destination visibility, matched rule, and override status. That lets the non-secret files copy while preventing one private key from becoming public.

If a deny rule is omitted, the test should fail before any tool call happens. Runtime denials should also name the matching rule so users can tell whether the subagent's own policy or the parent policy blocked it.

Loaded skills are part of the active context contract, so the sidebar should show more than a count. Useful fields: skill name, source path or package, loaded vs invoked, load trigger, token/byte estimate, and last refresh time. That makes skill context inspectable without forcing users into a debug command after the model has already acted on those instructions.

Emit periodic process metrics: rss, heap used/total, external memory, swap, active sessions, open streams, tool calls served, and uptime. Pair that with a leak guard that snapshots the last N session/tool events before restart, so the next report can tie growth to a workload pattern.

For large files, sample start, middle, and final bytes, plus file size and mtime if available; or use an incremental full hash when the file is already being read. A regression can edit only the final line of a large file and assert the viewer cache key changes before render.

The parent loop then records accept/reject per item, instead of asking the model to parse a blob and remember every detail. That also gives audits a durable trail for skipped items.

For invalid enum params, return schema path, bad value, allowed values, whether retry is safe, and the original tool call id. The model can then repair the next call deterministically, and logs can distinguish schema-invalid retries from tool runtime failures.

If bash exits cleanly but the next stream never reaches first byte, the session can fail with a recoverable stream_timeout instead of hanging indefinitely.

@Necmttn agreed — a destination-aware per-file guard (classify → copy / skip / ask, with a receipt covering source path, destination visibility, matched rule, override status) is the more robust fix, since it's an action-level check rather than relying on the model to self-restrain.
